clusters.name: Secondary school: clash with stepfather, anxiety over chess
clusters.reason: Around 1987, as Jonah began secondary school, three shifts piled up: distance hardened between him and his stepfather Desmond, while he stayed warm with his father Russell though hungry for his notice; his parents' marriage hit a rough patch when Desmond's wife left over the question of starting a family; and Jonah made the city chess squad but felt out of his depth, his anxiety rising. The period opens with these tensions in the family and Jonah's own struggle.

clusters.name: Late secondary and early university: grandfather's death, family rebuild, wrist injury, and withdrawal
clusters.reason: Between 1989 and early 1992, multiple shifts converged. Jonah's grandfather Clifford came back into the family after years away around 1989, a large family occasion. That same spring Desmond took a rental on Quarry Lane, and by autumn the rebuilt Hollin Road house was ready; the household was loud and cramped with Desmond's children. Jonah's late nights, which had been present before, shifted toward symptom around 1989. He dropped chess and debate as music took over. His sister Tara was born in 1990. He began university at Wexley Conservatory in 1991, choosing it because his closest friend Rafe was there, and the two fused. That October a wrist injury stopped his playing, his anxiety and functioning both falling; he and Rafe had a blow-up and Rafe moved out. Jonah withdrew into his room, getting high and absorbed in fixing radios. By early 1992, with his grandfather Gordon dead in June 1991 and his mother about to remarry, he was lost and low, unable to get going. The period names the piling of structural changes—rebuild, birth, university move, injury—and Jonah's shift from engagement to withdrawal and symptom.

clusters.name: Late 1990s: performing peak, insomnia, and first partnership ending
clusters.reason: Between early 1998 and mid-1999, two shifts that count frame a period of high performance alongside emerging symptom. Jonah bonded with Joelle in 1998. By 1999 his insomnia began getting in the way, particularly before concerts, even though he was playing the best he had ever had and winning competitions—his high point as a performer. That July he separated from Joelle; within weeks he started therapy with Victor Halloran, reading about families with a gambler and beginning to question his own inheritance. The period holds the contradiction: functioning at its peak and symptom rising at once, then the relationship ending and him turning toward help.

clusters.name: Early 2000s: burnout, failed audition, depression after separation, and grandmother's death
clusters.reason: Between 2001 and early 2004, multiple shifts and structural losses piled close together. In autumn 2001 Jonah's anxiety rose as he ran out of steam for performing, his functioning falling by the month. His grandmother Winifred was found to have bowel cancer around the same time, the year uncertain; she underwent operations and chemotherapy. In early 2002 Jonah had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra in his home town; he was done with performing and began casting about for what came next. He was on poor terms with family and friends, his distance from them widening. That autumn he left Thornbury for Gull Harbour. Early in 2003 he met Marisol at a winter party; by June he left Gull Harbour to live with her in Fenwick. By October they separated within the year. That winter he sank into a deep depression back in Thornbury, at the bottom, minding a house near Hamish and hardly moving from the sofa. He could not face his family; his parents seemed a world away. He relied, gingerly, on friends—Corbin, Dale, and Silas. His grandmother spent her final months in Maureen and Desmond's home; in January 2004 Jonah dropped in briefly, hung over, on the way to the airport, and that visit was their last. In February 2004 Winifred died. Around the same time, Jonah began swimming laps to help him sleep, requested help from his parents with therapy costs, and returned to Victor Halloran; the gradual recovery began there and pointed him toward nursing. The period opens with burnout at work and closes as he begins to recover through therapy and a new direction.

clusters.name: 2008–2010: nursing school, cutoff from mother, aunt's stroke, partners' children born
clusters.reason: Between early 2008 and early 2010, structural changes and relationship shifts converged. In January 2008 Jonah's grandmother Lorna died; his grandfather Clifford also died around this time, the year uncertain. That summer Jonah spent four weeks building at Alder Creek with Silas before nursing school began. His mother pressed him to visit him there; he told her repeatedly the timing was wrong, and she drove out regardless. The visit went wrong; she never got inside and he kept the door shut on her. When he left for nursing school in Marlow Sound that August, he stopped speaking to his mother; the silence held for roughly a year—a cutoff. Around the same time, his aunt Imogen had a stroke with months of rehabilitation. Between 2010 and 2012, his partner's brother Leo's children were born. The period opens with two deaths in the extended family, moves through the conflict with his mother and the cutoff, and holds the shifts in Jonah's functioning as he began nursing school.

clusters.name: 2017–2019: marriage, in-law integration, partner's overwhelm, and sleep trouble at family gatherings
clusters.reason: Between Jonah's marriage to Wren in March 2017 and autumn 2019, multiple shifts and structural changes piled up. When Wren came along, Jonah saw his mother a bit less; contact eased off slightly. His cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2017. His sister Tara married James; they live in Rennick for her work with a regional airline. His aunt Imogen's memory began slipping noticeably by 2018, getting worse; by late 2018 she was lashing out when muddled, her conflict with her son Hal rising. His job steadied in 2019, paying well, and his anxiety fell; but by October his constant feeling that he ought to drive his projects forward—his anxiety—rose again, and he started a sleeping pill. He aimed for shorter, more regular calls with his mother, his lesson from years before. His sister announced a baby on the way, Russell's first known grandchild. Then in late October 2019, multiple events converged: Wren was swamped, one thing after another—a street party, a fundraising dinner, then the drive to the lake for her mother Frances's retirement party. Jonah was too strict laying out a plan to settle her when she was swamped, his anxiety rising and his overfunctioning showing. Wren's family—her father Hugo, her brother Leo—talk all day; nothing happens to one that the others don't hear; they are fused. Once the weekend had a plan, Wren settled and the dinner went well. But at the lake house that weekend, Jonah was awake from the small hours, no more sleep, and could only pull back as the others rose; his symptom and anxiety both rose, and he withdrew from the group. Wren became anxious when he had no sleep at family occasions; long quiet drives home followed. The period opens with structural moves in the wider family and closes with Jonah's sleep and anxiety at their worst around Wren's family.
